narrationPlan.voice: One clear, warm narrator throughout; no character voices
narrationPlan.pace: Clear, steady, and thoughtful (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read as a single narrator: this is a science article, not a story with characters.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason first.
Say numbers and units in full ("one hundred and fifty million kilometres", "astronomical units") and pronounce names clearly.

teacherGuide.overview: Introduces the electromagnetic spectrum in order of wavelength, weighing the uses of each part against its risks.
learningGoals: Name the parts of the electromagnetic spectrum in order.
State that all electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in empty space.
Give one use and one danger of ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.
Explain simple ways to reduce exposure to harmful rays.

beforeReading: Ask: name something that reaches you from the Sun that you cannot see. Record the answers.
whileReading: After Page 2, learners line up holding cards for the seven parts of the spectrum in the right order.
afterReading: Learners make a two-column table: use and danger, for four parts of the spectrum.
discussion: Is it fair to call any kind of ray simply good or bad? Use two examples from the article.
reflection: What will you do differently on the next very sunny day?

mathsExtension.task: A communications satellite is 36,000 km above Earth. How long does a radio signal take to reach it at 300,000 km/s?
A pulsar spins 30 times each second. How many times does it spin in one minute?

support: Give learners a printed spectrum strip to colour and label as they read.
stretch: Find out who first detected a pulsar, in which year, and why the signal puzzled astronomers.
